sections.heading: Asking the Spirit to bring order to my heart
sections.text:
Holy Spirit, God who comes from the Father and the Son, have mercy on me.

At the beginning, you moved over the emptiness and confusion, and by God’s word the world took shape—ordered, beautiful, and full of life. Please move over my heart like that. Bring order where I am tangled up inside. Put to death the desires in me that pull against you, the cravings I excuse, and the sins I secretly protect. Clear away the fog of unbelief. Let the truth shine in me with clean, steady light.
theological_themes: The Holy Spirit is fully divine and active in creation and new creation.
The heart can be disordered by sin, unbelief, and unruly desire, and needs God’s merciful renewal.
The Spirit brings light, order, and life where there is darkness and confusion.

scripture_references.connection: The Spirit’s presence over the unformed creation grounds the prayer’s image of God bringing order and life out of chaos. The prayer applies that same life-giving work to the inner disorder of the human heart.
Paul describes salvation as involving renewal by the Holy Spirit, poured out through Jesus Christ. This supports asking the Spirit not merely to improve behavior, but to renew the person from within.

sections.heading: Asking to become fruitful and alive with grace
sections.text: Make my soul like a garden you have restored—alive, fruitful, and beautiful in ways that come from heaven, not from me. Let your grace make my life fragrant with what pleases you. Let your light reach the places in me that are still dim, hard, or hidden.
theological_themes: The Spirit produces real spiritual fruit in the believer’s life.
Grace changes not only outward conduct but the inward condition of the soul.
Holiness is beautiful because it reflects God’s own light and life.

scripture_references.connection: Paul identifies the character qualities the Spirit produces in believers. The prayer’s request for fruitfulness and beauty is a request for this Spirit-grown life rather than self-made moral polish.
This passage connects beholding the Lord’s glory with being transformed by the Spirit. It supports the prayer’s longing for inner brightness and increasing likeness to Christ.

sections.heading: Asking the Spirit to show me Christ
sections.text:
Please do in me all the work you love to do. Comfort me, teach me, guide me, make me holy. Take what belongs to Jesus and make it real to my heart.

Help me learn more of his love, his grace, his compassion, his faithfulness, and his beauty—not as ideas I can repeat, but as truth I actually know and live from.
theological_themes: The Spirit comforts, teaches, guides, and sanctifies believers.
The Spirit’s ministry is Christ-centered: he glorifies Christ and makes Christ known to the soul.
Growing knowledge of Christ is personal, transforming, and rooted in grace.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus says the Spirit will guide his people into truth and glorify him by taking what is his and declaring it to them. This directly grounds the prayer’s request that the Spirit show Christ to the soul.
Jesus calls the Holy Spirit the Helper who teaches and reminds his disciples of his words. That supports asking the Spirit to be comforter, light, and guide in an ongoing way.

sections.heading: Seeing my sin at the cross
sections.text:
Lead me to the cross and keep me there long enough to see the truth. Show me the wounds of Jesus. Show me how evil really looks when it is laid on the innocent Son of God. Show me the hatred of sin, the cruelty of Satan’s work, and the cost of my rebellion.

Do not let me look at the cross from a safe distance. Help me see that my sins were not small. They were like the nails, the ropes, the thorns, and the spear. I do not want to excuse what Christ died to bear.
theological_themes: The cross reveals both the seriousness of sin and the depth of Christ’s suffering love.
Personal sin is not treated lightly, because Christ bore sin in his body.
Satan’s work is exposed and defeated through Christ’s death.

scripture_references.connection: Isaiah presents the Servant as wounded for the sins of others, with the guilt of God’s people laid on him. This supports the prayer’s personal confession that Christ’s sufferings are connected to the worshiper’s own sin.
Peter teaches that Christ bore sins in his body on the tree so that believers might die to sin and live to righteousness. This grounds both the grief over sin and the desire to flee it.

Paul connects the cancellation of the believer’s debt with Christ’s public triumph over the rulers and authorities. This supports the prayer’s link between the cross, forgiven guilt, and Satan’s defeated power.

sections.heading: Resting in what Jesus finished
sections.text:
Help me find in Jesus’ death the true size of his love. Open up to me the wonder of his words, “It is finished.” Let me trust more deeply that the atonement has been made, the debt has been paid, the guilt has been removed, and nothing still needs to be added to make me right with you.

Because of Christ, my sins are forgiven, I have been bought back, my soul is safe, hell has been defeated, heaven has been opened, and eternal life is mine in him. Holy Spirit, press these saving truths deep into me until they become the ground under my feet.
theological_themes: Christ’s finished work is complete and sufficient for salvation.
The cross secures forgiveness, redemption, the removal of guilt, rescue from judgment, and the hope of eternal life.
Faith grows as the Spirit deepens confidence in what Christ has accomplished.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus’ cry, “It is finished,” marks the completion of the work the Father gave him to do. The prayer draws from this statement the believer’s confidence that salvation rests on Christ’s completed work, not unfinished human payment.

Hebrews contrasts repeated sacrifices with Christ’s single, effective offering. This supports the prayer’s confidence that atonement and cleansing are not partial or ongoing payments but decisively accomplished in Christ.
Paul joins redemption through Christ’s blood with the forgiveness of sins according to God’s grace. That directly supports the prayer’s assurance of debt paid, sins forgiven, and the person redeemed.

sections.heading: Learning to hate sin and love Christ
sections.text:
Holy Spirit, keep teaching me these saving truths. Write them on my heart, not just in my memory. Make my daily life one that hates sin, runs from sin, and loves Christ.

Do not let the devil trick me, flatter me, accuse me away from hope, or lead me back into what Jesus died to free me from. Keep me close to Christ, clear-minded about sin, and awake to your truth.
theological_themes: The Spirit internalizes gospel truth so that it shapes daily obedience.
True grace trains believers to hate and flee sin, not make peace with it.
Believers need God’s protection against deception, temptation, accusation, and spiritual warfare.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that believers put sinful deeds to death by the Spirit. This grounds the prayer’s request for a life that actively hates and flees sin through divine help.

Paul speaks of believers as a letter written by the Spirit on human hearts. This supports asking the Spirit to write saving truths deeply into the inner person, not merely leave them as external information.
Paul warns believers to stand against the devil’s schemes. This supports the prayer’s final request not to be deceived or drawn away by spiritual opposition.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The opening line says the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, reflecting the Western doctrine often called the filioque. This is historically contested between Eastern Orthodox and Western Christian traditions, so it was preserved without expanding or arguing the point.

The prayer’s language connecting the speaker’s sins with the nails, cords, thorns, and spear is intense and penitential. It can be misunderstood as literal historical causation, so the adaptation renders it as a theological and moral identification with the sin Christ bore.
The references to Satan and hell were preserved because they are central to the original’s biblical worldview and not merely decorative imagery.
significant_interpretive_choices: “Move upon my disordered heart” was interpreted as an intentional echo of the Spirit hovering over the waters in Genesis 1:2, applied to inner renewal and sanctification rather than to creation alone.
“The glory of thy divine offices” was rendered as the Spirit doing his work as comforter, teacher, guide, and sanctifier, since the following line in the original names those roles.

“Open for me the wondrous volumes of truth in his, ‘It is finished’” was interpreted as asking the Spirit to unfold the many saving implications of Christ’s completed work, including atonement, forgiveness, redemption, victory, and eternal hope.
